nodes.title: Windows administration: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Windows admin questions cluster around a few core tools: Settings, Control Panel, Task Manager, Event Viewer, the Registry, and Group Policy. Knowing which tool owns which knob saves you in scenario questions where every distractor 'kind of' fits.

flashcards.front: When do you use Group Policy vs the Registry directly?
flashcards.back: Group Policy is the supported, centrally-managed way to enforce settings on domain-joined machines — auditable, reversible, scoped to OUs. Editing the Registry directly works on any machine but is per-host, undocumented, and easy to break. Use GPO for domain config; use Registry edits only for one-off targeted fixes with a backup first.

flashcards.front: What does Event Viewer show?
flashcards.back: Windows' centralized log: Application logs (apps), Security logs (auth attempts, audit events), System logs (driver/service errors). Filter by Event ID — most exam scenarios give you an ID number and ask which log to check. Save a custom view for the events your team cares about.

flashcards.front: Task Manager vs Resource Monitor vs Performance Monitor.
flashcards.back: Task Manager: instant snapshot of CPU/RAM/disk/network usage per process — first stop for 'why is my machine slow?'. Resource Monitor: deeper per-resource view with handles and modules. Performance Monitor: long-term metric collection and alerts (set up Data Collector Sets to record over time).

flashcards.front: How do you join a PC to an Active Directory domain?
flashcards.back: Settings → System → About → Rename this PC (advanced) → Change → choose Domain → enter domain name → authenticate with a domain account that has join rights → reboot. The PC gets an AD computer object, group policy starts applying, domain users can log in.

nodes.title: PC hardware: Key Ideas
nodes.content: CompTIA A+ and similar exams test physical hardware: connectors, motherboard layout, power, storage, RAM types. The trick is matching the symptom to the component — boot failures usually mean RAM/power/CMOS battery, slow disk means thermals or imminent failure.

flashcards.front: DDR3 vs DDR4 vs DDR5 — what changes?
flashcards.back: Each generation roughly doubles peak bandwidth and lowers operating voltage. DDR3 = 1.5V, DDR4 = 1.2V, DDR5 = 1.1V. Slots are keyed differently — you cannot physically install the wrong generation. Mixing speeds in dual-channel makes them run at the slowest speed.

flashcards.front: M.2 NVMe vs M.2 SATA vs 2.5" SATA — which is fastest?
flashcards.back: M.2 NVMe (uses PCIe lanes): 3,500-7,000 MB/s read. M.2 SATA (M.2 form factor but SATA bus): ~550 MB/s. 2.5" SATA: also ~550 MB/s. The same M.2 slot may accept both; the motherboard manual tells you which keys (B-key SATA, M-key NVMe) it supports.

flashcards.front: What does the CMOS battery do?
flashcards.back: Powers the CMOS chip that stores BIOS/UEFI settings and the real-time clock when the system is unplugged. Symptoms of a dead one: clock resets to default on every boot, BIOS settings revert, occasional 'CMOS checksum error'. Coin cell CR2032, $1 fix.

flashcards.front: POST beep codes — what do they mean?
flashcards.back: Power-On Self-Test diagnostic beeps from the motherboard speaker before video init. Single short beep = pass. Repeating short beeps = memory error. Long-short-short = video problem. Each BIOS vendor has a slightly different code chart — check the motherboard manual.

pairs.stem: What is the purpose of thermal paste on a CPU?
pairs.option: Fills microscopic gaps between the CPU and heatsink to improve thermal conductivity

nodes.title: Storage concepts: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud storage comes in three flavors with very different cost/perf trade-offs: object (think S3), block (think EBS / managed disks), and file (think EFS / Azure Files / Filestore). Pick wrong and you either overpay or hit performance ceilings.

flashcards.front: Object vs block vs file storage — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Object (S3, Blob, GCS) for unstructured data, backups, static sites, data lakes — flat namespace, HTTP API, infinite scale. Block (EBS, managed disks) for OS disks and databases — low latency, single attach. File (EFS, NFS) when multiple VMs need a shared POSIX filesystem.

flashcards.front: What is a storage class / tier?
flashcards.back: Same data, different SLA and price. Hot tier (frequent access, expensive read, cheap retrieval). Cold/archive tier (rare access, cheap to store, expensive to read, retrieval latency from minutes to hours). Lifecycle policies move data between tiers automatically.

flashcards.front: Why use server-side encryption?
flashcards.back: Data is encrypted at rest by the storage service using either provider-managed keys (default, no extra config) or your own keys via KMS. This protects against physical disk theft and meets compliance baselines without changing your app code.

flashcards.front: What's storage durability vs availability?
flashcards.back: Durability is the chance your data won't be lost (object stores claim ~11 9s — 99.999999999%). Availability is the chance you can reach it right now (typically 4 9s — 99.99%). Durability is multi-region replication; availability is how many concurrent failures the service tolerates.

pairs.stem: What does RAID 1 provide?
pairs.option: Mirroring — exact copy of data on two drives for redundancy

pairs.stem: What does S.M.A.R.T. technology do for hard drives?
What is the difference between MBR and GPT disk partitioning?
What is 'imaging' a drive in IT support?
pairs.option: Creating a sector-by-sector exact copy of an entire drive — including OS, partitions, and data — for backup, cloning, or forensics

pairs.stem: What is the purpose of disk defragmentation and should you defrag an SSD?
pairs.option: HDDs: defrag consolidates fragmented files so the read head travels less — improves performance. SSDs: NEVER manually defrag — TRIM handles optimization and defragging causes unnecessary write cycles reducing lifespan. Windows auto-schedules correctly

nodes.title: Troubleshooting methodology: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A structured troubleshooting process beats random guessing every time. The classic flow: identify the problem precisely, form a theory, test it, fix, verify, document. Most exams test that you know the flow AND can spot the layer at which the symptom originates.

flashcards.front: What's the standard troubleshooting model?
flashcards.back: CompTIA's 6-step: (1) Identify the problem (gather symptoms, questions to user, recent changes). (2) Establish a theory of probable cause. (3) Test the theory. (4) Plan and implement the fix. (5) Verify full system functionality, apply preventive measures. (6) Document everything.

flashcards.front: Top-down vs bottom-up troubleshooting on a network problem.
flashcards.back: Top-down: start at the application layer and work down — does the browser work? DNS? TCP? Routing? Bottom-up: start at the physical layer — is the cable plugged in? Link light? IP? When you suspect physical/cable, bottom-up is faster. When the user has 'a website is broken', top-down is faster.

flashcards.front: Why ask 'what changed recently'?
flashcards.back: Almost every production incident traces back to a recent change — a deploy, a config push, a vendor patch, a cert rotation. 'It was working yesterday' tells you to check today's change-log before forming an exotic theory. Recent changes are the highest-priors of the bug space.

flashcards.front: What's the divide-and-conquer technique?
flashcards.back: Bisect the path between symptom and cause. If 10 hops between client and server, test hop 5. Good → problem is past hop 5. Bad → problem is before. Two more bisections narrow it to one hop. Faster than checking every link sequentially when the chain is long.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

pairs.stem: What is the function of DNS in everyday computing?
pairs.option: Translates human-readable domain names (www.google.com) to IP addresses — without DNS, you'd need to memorize IP addresses for every website. Operates hierarchically: root → TLD (.com/.net) → authoritative DNS

What does ESD stand for and why is it a concern for technicians?

pairs.stem: What is the difference between a virus and a worm?
pairs.option: Virus: requires a host file and human action to spread. Worm: self-replicates and spreads automatically over networks without human interaction (exploits vulnerabilities)
